title: decode-stage preempt & stitch benchmark notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures an experimental sweep exploring the interaction between decode-stage preemption (preempting an in-flight token stream to schedule a higher-priority request) and stitch/merge cost when serving streaming responses. The goal: measure p50/p90/p99 latency impact, per-request GPU token cost, and the stitch overhead that appears when multiplexing preempted streams back together (e.g., concatenating emitted chunks or reusing KV cache slices).

Why this matters:
- Many customer workloads are long tail (variable-length streaming) where urgent small requests can interrupt large streaming responses.
- We need a principled metric to trade faster response for small, high-priority requests vs. total token-cost blowups and p99 regressions for affected long sessions.
- This intersects with routing/fallback policies and slot allocation heuristics in Dedicated.

Experiment Design:
- Hardware: 8xA100 logical testbed (single GPU chosen per slot for reproducibility).
- Model: open-quantized variant of M-13B (approx 13B dense equiv) to reflect typical mid-size customer models.
- Runtime config: two scheduling modes tested: (A) Preemptive-pause: pause low-priority decode, run high-priority request, then resume. (B) Non-preemptive-drain: allow current decode to finish chunk then start high-priority request.
- Stitch strategies after preemption: (1) naive-concat: resume and stream remaining tokens as new chunk; (2) kv-resume: restore KV cache and continue as if uninterrupted (best-effort); (3) mini-reset: restart decoding low-priority request from last stable checkpoint (higher cost but deterministic).
- Workloads: synthetic mix derived from production session traces: 70% short queries (<32 tokens), 20% medium (32–256 tokens), 10% long (>256 tokens). Preemption events triggered at randomized points in long sessions to mimic real interrupts.
- Measure: latency seen by high-priority requests (p50/p90/p99), extra tokens decoded (measured as delta GPU-token time), observed p99 degradation for low-priority sessions, and end-to-end streaming coherency issues (percent of responses needing stitch-fixup).

Microbench results (representative numbers):

1) High-priority latency (ms) observed under different scheduler modes (mixed load; numbers averaged over 10k high-priority samples):

Mode            | p50  | p90  | p99
----------------|------|------|-----
Non-preemptive  | 45   | 92   | 240
Preemptive-pause| 18   | 35   | 110

Interpretation: preemption reduces end-to-end latency for urgent requests by ~60–70% at p50/p90. P99 still higher due to occasional long stalls (cache restores).

2) Per-request token cost delta (extra tokens decoded per preempted long session):

Stitch strategy  | extra tokens per preemption (median) | cost note
------------------|-------------------------------------|---------------------------
naive-concat      | +0.2 tokens                          | minimal; just stream continuation
kv-resume         | +4.6 tokens                          | cache rehydration/duplicate decoding window
mini-reset        | +12.0 tokens                         | re-decode from last checkpoint, worse for deep contexts

3) Low-priority session p99 impact (ms): measured as p99 end-to-end latency after X preemptions per minute

Preemptions/min | p99 non-preemptive | p99 preemptive-pause (kv-resume)
-----------------|---------------------|-------------------------------
0                | 240                 | 240
6                | 270                 | 360
12               | 330                 | 520

Interpretation: under moderate to high preemption rates, preemptive with kv-resume amplifies p99 latency for long sessions because KV restore/overlap increases decoding contention; non-preemptive shows smoother growth but higher latency for urgent requests.

ASCII chart: extra-token cost vs preemptions/min (median extra tokens per long session):

Preemptions/min: 0   3   6   9   12
naive-concat:     0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3 0.4
kv-resume:        0.0 1.2 4.6 7.9 12.3
mini-reset:       0.0 2.8 12.0 22.5 34.1

Notes on measurement fidelity:
- We instrumented both runtime internal counters (KV restore time, decode retries) and client-observed timings. There's an observed ~5% sampling penalty for tracing enabled; numbers above are corrected for that bias.
- Stitch correctness: kv-resume produced the fewest visible artifacts in output coherence (0.7% of preemptions required manual stitch-fixup), naive-concat had 1.6% fidelity anomalies, mini-reset had 0% correctness issues but highest cost.

Qualitative observations:
- KV-resume is attractive: good balance of correctness and latency for moderate preemption rates (<6/min). However, it induces contention on the decode pipeline: multiple short-lived KV restores create localized bursts in GPU memory and kernel selection churn.
- naive-concat is cheap but manifests visible chunked continuity in conversational flows (clients may see abrupt tone change or minor overlap). For non-critical streaming (e.g., non-chat embeddings) it is fine.
- mini-reset provides deterministic outputs and easiest post-hoc debugging at cost of significant extra compute; could be acceptable for debug modes or SLAs that prioritize determinism.

Recommendations (short-term):
- Default scheduling: hybrid policy — allow preemption but prefer naive-concat when long session is in a low-coherence region (detected via low mutual info between chunks) and use kv-resume when session coherence score > threshold.
- Add a preemption budget per slot (tokens/minute) to cap worst-case p99 blowups across aggregated tenants. 6 preemptions/min per slot appears to be an inflection point in our tests for kv-resume.
- Expose a customer-facing knob: "prioritized-restore=best-effort|guaranteed|cheap" mapping to naive/kv/minireset strategies.

Recommendations (long-term / product):
- Instrument coherence score in the console (Optimize) and surface recommended stitch behavior per model and route. This lets users choose correctness vs cost.
- Consider a lightweight virtualized-KV approach: snapshot small KV deltas instead of full restore to reduce duplicate decode windows. Prototype micro-snapshotting in the runtime (low-risk experiment).
- Research area: kernel-level concurrency control to avoid KV restore thrash. Possibly gate restores via admission control that smooths memory allocations over 50–200ms windows.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do these measurements change on larger models (70B+) where KV size and restore time scale differently? Hypothesis: kv-resume cost multiplier increases superlinearly; naive-concat advantage grows.
- What is user tolerance for minor stitch artifacts in chat vs multi-turn SQL generation flows? Need UX experiments with a handful of customers (CS-led).
- Evaluate effect of preemption under multiplexed slotization (multiple small sessions sharing the same GPU slot).

Appendix A — experiment commands and flags:
- runtime flags: --sched=preemptive-pause --stitch=kv-resume --kv-snapshot=false --trace-level=sampled
- workload driver: tools/burstsim/run_mix --rng-seed=20281105 --mix-file=prod-synth-2028-11.json --interrupt-ps=0.1

Appendix B — quick decision matrix (for product/console teams):
- Low-cost priority (mobile push notifications): naive-concat
- High-fidelity multi-turn assistant: kv-resume with preemption budget
- Reproducible debug runs: mini-reset

End of note.
